title: T1595.002 — Active Scanning - Vulnerability Scanning
subtitle: Watch a Log4Shell-style probe: the scanner tests a Java app, the vulnerable app calls out, and the SOC watches the callback that proves everything.
aria: Simulation. Step 1: Prepare the probe list. After the Log4Shell vulnerability became public in December 2021, attackers built lists of internet-facing Java applications and started checking every one of them.

steps.caption: After the Log4Shell vulnerability became public in December 2021, attackers built lists of internet-facing Java applications and started checking every one of them.
steps.defender: Vulnerability scanning spikes right after a CVE is published. Subscribe to advisories so your patching starts the same day, not the same month.

steps.title: Fingerprint candidates
steps.caption: The scanner sends normal-looking requests and reads the answers. Response headers and error pages reveal that the target runs Java, which makes it interesting.
steps.defender: Fingerprinting looks almost like normal browsing. What stands out is the source: one IP asking many different servers the same small set of questions.

steps.title: Send the crafted probe
steps.caption: The scanner hides a special string in a request header. If the app logs it, the log4j library tries to resolve the embedded address - that is the vulnerability test.
steps.defender: WAF and web logs can show these probe strings. Alerting on ${jndi: in any logged field catches both scanning and real exploitation attempts.

steps.title: The app calls out
steps.caption: The vulnerable application resolves the attacker domain through the company DNS resolver. A server looking up a fresh domain is already suspicious on its own.
steps.defender: Egress DNS from servers should be rare and allowlisted. A lookup of a domain registered days ago is a high-value signal.

steps.title: Callback lands
steps.caption: The resolver connects onward to the attacker listener. This callback proves the target is vulnerable. Scanning has now become confirmed exploitation.
steps.defender: This is the detection point that matters: egress from a web tier to a strange LDAP or DNS endpoint. Even one hit deserves a page, not just a ticket.

steps.title: Mark the target vulnerable
steps.caption: The attacker records the target as vulnerable. In the real campaign, thousands of servers were added to lists like this within days of disclosure.
steps.defender: Assume any host that called out is compromised until proven otherwise. Preserve logs and start incident response, do not just patch quietly.

steps.title: SOC hunts the campaign
steps.caption: The SOC searches the last day of logs for the same pattern: probe strings in web logs and odd outbound lookups. They find several scanners and one callback.
steps.defender: Hunting turns one alert into a story: how many probes, which sources, did anything call out. Share the query with peers so others can check fast.

steps.title: Patch, block, verify
steps.caption: The team deploys the fixed log4j version, adds a WAF rule as a stopgap, and tightens egress so callbacks cannot leave. A re-scan a day later shows the technique no longer works.
steps.defender: Verification closes the loop: re-run the detection, confirm the egress block, and add the whole pattern to your regression tests for future CVE waves.
